recentItems.title: The imminent encryption crisis | Samantha Lowrimore | TEDxUniversityofMississippi
recentItems.description:
Cyber threats like Q-Day and entropic warfare are emerging with a new technilogical era. Our old methods of security are vulnerable. That's where EISD comes in. Entropy as Infrustructure for Security and Defense is a new, hacker-created field striving to keep us safe.

#EISD #quantum #entropy SAMANTHA LOWRIMORE, known as CyberSamantha, is an ethical hacker, entropy advocate, founder of PostQuantSec.io, and one of the first recognized quantum hackers working to secure life beyond Earth and the quantum horizon. A cybersecurity engineer, her work begins with quantum-era security and extends beyond, spanning quantum cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, satellites, and interplanetary computing. She is helping to build the foundations that will safeguard the next generation of human and machine intelligence across worlds. Through her research and pioneering of the Lowrimore Approach to Quantum Migration, she is redefining how global leaders understand security, resilience, and ethics at the edge of the expanding digital frontier. 

This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Are you a battery charger? | Marc Byrnes | TEDxHunting Valley
recentItems.description: Marc Byrnes asks one question three times, and by the third time you realize he is asking about you. Battery chargers empower the people around them; battery drainers want to be king of the castle. Six decades of mentors, setbacks, a company rebuilt around one word, and one formula: IQ minus EQ equals Miss Q. Marc Byrnes is Chairman Emeritus of Oswald Companies, one of the country's largest employee-owned insurance brokers, which he led beginning in 1996, rebuilding a 103-year-old firm of 40 people around one word, caring, and growing it into 1,400 employee-owners. He has chaired the United Way of Greater Cleveland and serves on the boards of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and University School, and Inside Business has named him one of the 100 most influential leaders in Northeast Ohio. He is University School Class of 1972, and at 72 he coaches the school's freshman football team. His talk asks one question three times: are you a battery charger, or a battery drainer? His answer draws on six decades of mentors, setbacks, and second families, and on one formula: IQ minus EQ equals Miss Q. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Breaking Out | Brandon Chrostowski | TEDxHunting Valley
recentItems.description: Nationally, two-thirds of people released from prison are rearrested within three years. At EDWINS, the number is a fraction of that. Chef Brandon Chrostowski shares the engine behind it: nobody is asked what they did, only who they want to become, and every base need, from an ID to housing to childcare, is covered. Same human, same prison, different engine, different result. Brandon Chrostowski trained as a chef and sommelier in Paris, New York, and Chicago before founding EDWINS Leadership and Restaurant Institute in Cleveland, which gives formerly incarcerated adults free culinary and hospitality training alongside housing, childcare, a fitness center, a butcher shop, a bakery, and a diner. Its tablet-based curriculum now reaches prisons in 49 states with more than 70,000 graduates, and its alumni return to prison at a fraction of the national rate. He is a CNN Hero and a James Beard Impact Award honoree, and the documentary about his work, Knife Skills, was nominated for an Academy Award. His talk, “Breaking Out,” starts on a Paris park bench the night before his first shift at a three-Michelin-star restaurant, and builds to the question EDWINS asks instead of “what did you do?”: who do you want to become? This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: It’s About What You Say, Not How You Say It | James Mason Jr. | TEDxHunting Valley
recentItems.description: On the first day of ninth grade, James Mason Jr. walked into English class with six months of memorized vocabulary, ready to prove that how you say something matters most. The praise never came, so he kept adjusting, building a different James for every room. Drawing on W.E.B. Du Bois, he draws the line between adaptation, which lets us connect, and conformity, which asks us to disappear. James Mason Jr. is a senior at University School, one of ten elected House Prefects, State Runner-Up in Poetry Out Loud, a Sherman Prize finalist, a state qualifier in the shot put, and a graduate of the inaugural Cleveland Cavaliers Social Impact Academy. His talk, “It's About What You Say, Not How You Say It,” begins on the first day of ninth grade, with six months of memorized vocabulary and a teacher's praise that never came. From there he traces code switching, the different James he built for every classroom, to W.E.B. Du Bois's 1903 idea of double consciousness, and draws a hard line between adaptation, which lets us connect, and conformity, which asks us to disappear. He ends by flipping the phrase he was raised on completely upside down. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: The Cost of Caring | Melissa Kaiser | TEDxFargo
recentItems.description:
NOTE FROM TED: This talk contains a discussion of child sexual abuse, trafficking, and related traumatic experiences. Please do not look to this talk as a substitute for mental health advice and seek professional help if you are struggling. Contents only represent the speaker’s personal views and experiences. TEDx events are independently organized by volunteers. The guidelines we give TEDx organizers are described in more detail here: http://storage.ted.com/tedx/manuals/tedx_content_guidelines.pdf

Caring for others changes us. But what happens when we carry too much of other people's pain?

Vicarious trauma is the emotional impact of repeated exposure to the suffering of others. Often associated with first responders and helping professionals, its effects can extend into everyday life, quietly changing how we see safety, trust, relationships, and hope.

Drawing from fifteen years in anti-human trafficking work, Melissa Kaiser explores what it means to absorb other people's pain over time, and why so many people who care for others carry that weight in silence.

Melissa introduces The Alignment Zone (TAZ), the space where what matters most overlaps with what is within our control. Through practical strategies for honesty, rest, connection, reflection, and grounding, she challenges the idea that strength means being unaffected.

Because being changed by the pain of others doesn't mean we're broken. It means we're human. And learning how to set that burden down may be one of the most important ways we can continue to care for others without losing ourselves. Melissa Kaiser is a nationally recognized consultant, trainer, and speaker specializing in anti-human trafficking, multidisciplinary team building, and wellness for professionals in high-trauma fields. With over 15 years as a social worker, she has worked alongside first responders and helping professionals to improve victim outcomes through trauma-informed, person-centered practices. She pioneered a human trafficking and victim/witness program and has helps rescue missing and exploited children across the country. Melissa was a nominee for YWCA’s Women of the Year and is the voice behind Secrets of a Social Worker (swsecrets.net), where she shares honest insights on resilience, growth, and the human side of helping others. Her mission is to help those who protect and serve others remain resilient, connected, and effective while spreading kindness, offering support, and making someone’s day whenever she can. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: The Ads on Your Phone Are Making You Mow Your Lawn | Gage Martin | TEDxHunting Valley
recentItems.description: Why is your quality as a neighbor measured in inches of grass? Because two developers in the 1800s told you so. Gage Martin follows the false need from the suburban lawn to product placement, the beauty industry, and the manufactured need for constant connection, and offers a rule of thumb for spotting the needs somebody sold you. Gage Martin is a senior at Louisville High School and president of a speech and debate team he has competed on for seven years, ranking among the top competitors in Ohio. He is a member of the Ohio Department of Health's Teen Wellness Team and the creator of the nationally recognized Duck Game, digging into corporate influence on culture. His talk, “The Ads on Your Phone Are Making You Mow Your Lawn,” starts with his neighbor Mr. George and a question: why is your quality as a neighbor measured in inches of grass? The answer runs from two 19th-century developers who marketed the lawn as status, through philosopher Herbert Marcuse's idea of false needs, to product placement, the beauty industry, and social media's manufactured need for constant connection, and ends with a rule of thumb for spotting the needs somebody sold you. He still mows every Sunday. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: How efficiency erodes empathy | Priyasha Ghosal | TEDxHunting Valley
recentItems.description: A phone at 4 percent, a DoorDash order, a charger at the hotel door in thirty minutes: it felt like magic. Priyasha Ghosal asks who the magician really is, and shows how friction cannot be erased, only moved onto the people we no longer have to see. Her answer is intentional friction: a three-second pause between wanting something and tapping for it. Priyasha Ghosal is a sophomore at Hawken School. At twelve she founded Light of Love, a 501(c)(3) supporting pediatric cancer patients at St. Jude and Rainbow Babies. She is a nationally recognized math competitor, a competitive dancer, and a national debate semifinalist, and she led sixteen teens to raise more than $22,000 for cardiac disease awareness in eight weeks. Her talk, “The Human Cost of Convenience,” starts with a 9:32 PM DoorDash order and asks who the magician behind instant gratification really is. Her argument: friction cannot be erased, only moved, and what we call convenience is human labor we no longer have to witness. She closes with the case for intentional friction, a three-second pause between wanting and tapping that keeps our patience, and our empathy, human. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Where do we draw the line? Gerrymandering and democracy | Claire Witalec | TEDxHunting Valley
recentItems.description: Voters are supposed to pick their politicians. In redistricting, politicians pick their voters. Claire Witalec shows how packing and cracking quietly decide elections before a ballot is cast, why both parties do it, and what an ordinary citizen can actually do about it, starting this week. Claire Witalec is a rising junior at Laurel School in Shaker Heights, Ohio. She is a Democracy Summer Fellow, a research intern at the Matriots, the founder of Laurel's Girl Up chapter, and a Lincoln-Douglas debater working to grow young people's civic participation and turnout. She has cold-emailed Ohio state legislators with questions about voting and representation, and they met with her. Her talk, “Where Do We Draw the Line?,” traces gerrymandering from an 1812 Massachusetts map to the districts drawn around today's voters, shows how both parties use packing and cracking to pick their own electorates, and argues that redistricting is not a Democrats versus Republicans issue but a people versus politicians one, ending with what any citizen can actually do about it. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Feed billions, kill millions: The tragedy of Fritz Haber | Jackson Sarver | TEDxHunting Valley
recentItems.description: A 19th-century war over islands of bird guano, a German chemist who pulled fertilizer out of thin air, and the same molecule turned into weapons: half the people alive owe their existence to Fritz Haber’s ammonia, and millions died from it. Jackson Sarver traces the double life of one invention and asks whether our moral progress can keep pace with our technical progress, from chlorine gas to the dead zone that returns to Lake Erie every summer. Jackson Sarver is a senior at Aurora High School, a four-year varsity golfer, Student Council President, and a lover of science and history. His talk, “Feed Billions, Kill Millions,” follows the strangest thread in modern chemistry: a 19th-century war fought over islands of bird guano, the German chemist Fritz Haber whose ammonia synthesis now feeds roughly half the people on Earth, and the same molecule's dark record in chemical warfare, industrial disaster, and the dead zones that return to Lake Erie every year. It is a story about the race between technological advancement and moral advancement, and why the next great invention may be as capable of taking lives as saving them. His ideal afternoon is Barnes & Noble, the driving range, and old vinyl at his great-aunt's house. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Live Performance by a Country Artist | Sarah Gerald | TEDxCool Springs Youth
recentItems.description:

We were honored to have her be part of our inaugural event and to end the evening with such an authentic and memorable performance. North Carolina native turned Nashville resident, Sarah Gerald embodies the perfect blend of Southern roots and modern country. Hailing from a small town where country music was woven into everyday life, she has crafted a sound that honors tradition while embracing today’s country landscape.

As she continues to make her mark on the country music scene, her latest single, “Party Anywhere,” is available now on all streaming platforms. recentItems.title: The Power of Imagination | Akein Randeniya | TEDxKandy
recentItems.description:
Imagination is where every great idea begins. Before something becomes an invention, a story, a piece of art, or a dream for the future, it first exists in someone’s mind.
“The Power of Imagination” explores how our ability to imagine can help us see possibilities beyond what already exists. As children, we naturally dream, create, and ask “What if?” But as we grow older, fear of failure, expectations, and the pressure to be realistic can sometimes make us stop imagining.
This speech invites us to rediscover that sense of curiosity and wonder. It explores how imagination can help us solve problems, create new ideas, understand different perspectives, and envision a better future.
Because imagination is not simply about dreaming of what could be—it is the first step toward making what seems impossible possible. Akein Randeniya is a young and enthusiastic student from St. Anthony’s College, Kandy, with a strong passion for public speaking and drama. He enjoys expressing ideas, performing on stage, and connecting with audiences through confident communication and storytelling.
His love for drama has given him an appreciation for creativity, character, and different perspectives, while public speaking has helped him develop his confidence and ability to communicate meaningful ideas.
Making his TEDx debut, Akein brings the fresh perspective and enthusiasm of a young speaker who is eager to learn, explore, and inspire. He hopes to use this opportunity to encourage others to step beyond their comfort zones, find their voice, and have the courage to share their ideas. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

recentItems.title: Capacity: Reaching Untapped Strength | Ashley Fournet | TEDxCNU
recentItems.description:
We’ve all been told to “find balance.” Balance between work and life. Between ambition and rest. Between taking care of others and taking care of ourselves. It’s become the modern mantra for how to survive adulthood — as if we can somehow level out the chaos of real life with the right planner, the right morning routine, or the right podcast.

But here’s the truth: balance isn’t real. At least, not in the way we talk about it. Life doesn’t sit still long enough for equilibrium. It tilts. Constantly. And while we keep chasing the idea of perfect balance, we end up exhausted — not from doing too much, but from trying to control something that can’t be controlled.

My big idea challenges this obsession with balance and reframes it around a concept I call capacity. Capacity is not about keeping things even; it’s about building the strength to handle what’s uneven. It’s the mental, emotional, and physical bandwidth we create to navigate what life actually is — unpredictable, demanding, and beautifully chaotic. Dr. Ashley Fournet is a management professor who cares deeply about helping people grow — in the classroom, in their careers, and in their everyday lives. She teaches Human Resources and Organizational Behavior at Christopher Newport University, where her classes are less about memorizing business terms and more about figuring out what it really means to lead, communicate, and show up well for other people.

Ashley is known for being direct, real, and deeply invested in her students. She advises two student-led organizations — Women in Business and the CNU Next — where she mentors emerging leaders and helps them connect their ideas to impact. Her favorite moments are when students start to believe in their own potential and learn to push through the hard stuff with purpose.

Outside of the university, Ashley coaches at her local CrossFit gym, where the lessons often sound a lot like the ones she teaches in class: effort matters, feedback fuels growth, and consistency beats motivation every time. Before entering academia, she worked in sales, marketing, and event planning — experiences that taught her how to adapt fast, connect with people, and keep a sense of humor when things go sideways. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx
